newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian MPs fight over Deputy PM Di Rupo's future.
newsitem.headline: Belgian MPs fight over Deputy PM Di Rupo's future.

text.p: A special Belgian parliamentary commission squabbled into the night over the future of Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, who is alleged to have had sex with under-age boys.

The Francophone Socialist has already been cleared of allegations in one case that he had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 and he denies the mostly anonymous charges in two other instances.
"The mood is not good at all. We are far from a compromise," Flemish Socialist Louis Vanvelthoven told Reuters.

The 11-member commission, which has been sitting for three days, must decide whether to reject the charges, ask for more investigations or indict the number two in the government -- which would force his resignation.
Any decision must be endorsed by the full parliament.
The wrangling has already revealed strains in the governing centre-left coalition.
Di Rupo's own party and its sister Flemish Socialists say there is no case to answer. The opposition, led by the French- and Dutch-speaking Liberals, are calling for his head.
"We are certainly not going to drop this case," Gerolf Annemans of the opposition Flemish Union told Reuters.
In the middle are the Francophone and Flemish Christian Democrats who together with the Socialists form the coalition.

But the commission did agree a draft law that short-circuits the cumbersome parliamentary process and allows the Cour de Cassation to investigate allegations against a minister without needing permission from parliament.
The Cour de Cassation is Belgium's highest court and the only body allowed to investigate a government minister.
In the climate of suspicion in Belgium between the judiciary and politicians, and with deep public distrust of the system, this is equivalent to parliamentarians declaring open season on themselves.

The Di Rupo case has further undermined already weak public confidence, shaken since the arrest in August of child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four more.

More than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in October in support of the victims' families in a demonstration that united the country's divided linguistic communities and became a show of disgust at a system seen as corrupt.
There have also been floods of denunciations, with child rights groups reporting hundreds of letters a day and thousands of calls to a special police hot line.
In response, the government has rushed through a series of legal reforms and political leaders have begun a process that should lead to long-awaited democratic changes.

But Belgian politics received another blow on Monday when Jean-Pierre Grafe, a minister in a French-speaking regional government who has also been accused of paedophilia, unexpectedly announced his resignation.
He said he was innocent but could not continue to function in the current over-heated climate.
